title: Khoresh karafs
subtitle: Persian celery and lamb stew with herbs
excerpt: Khoresh karafs is one of the subtler Persian stews: tender lamb braised with a mountain of celery, flat-leaf parsley, and fresh mint until everything melts together into a pale, fragrant braise. The celery loses its crunch and takes on the lamb's flavour while retaining its own clean, grassy note.
sourceNotes: A Persian khoresh (stew) built around celery, which is one of the few green vegetables that holds up well to long, slow braising. Traditional across Iran and in the Iranian diaspora.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The stew improves overnight in the fridge. Make up to 2 days ahead.

content.text: Khoresh karafs is the Persian stew that converts celery sceptics. An entire head of celery goes into the pot and vanishes into the braise over two hours, turning from crisp and mildly bitter to silky and sweet, carrying the lamb's flavour into every piece.

The herbal element is substantial: a large bunch of flat-leaf parsley and a generous handful of mint go in with the celery, adding freshness to what could otherwise be a one-note stew. Lemon juice at the end sharpens everything.
Serve over plain white rice or basmati polo and offer yoghurt alongside. The stew is light enough for everyday eating and interesting enough for guests.

items.prepNote: steeped in 2 tbsp hot water, optional

content.text: Brown the lamb and soften the onion

Melt the butter in a heavy casserole over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook for 6 minutes until golden. Push to the edges and brown the lamb pieces in batches, 4 minutes per batch, until coloured on all sides. Return all the lamb to the pot. Add the turmeric and stir for 1 minute.

Add the celery, parsley, mint, stock, salt, and saffron water if using. Stir well to combine. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 1 to 1.5 hours until the lamb is tender and the celery has completely softened. The stew will look very green and the celery will have collapsed into the sauce.
Stir in the lemon juice and taste. Adjust the salt. The stew should be mildly tart from the lemon. Serve over plain basmati rice with yoghurt alongside.

items.symptom: Celery remains crunchy after cooking time
items.cause: Too little liquid or heat too low
items.fix: Add another 100 ml of stock and continue simmering covered for 20 more minutes.

items.cause: Celery released extra water during cooking
items.fix: Uncover for the last 20 minutes of cooking to reduce the liquid.

items.cause: Under-seasoned or lemon juice not added
items.fix: The lemon is critical; the stew tastes flat without it. Add gradually and taste.

content.text: Some versions use veal or chicken instead of lamb. Fresh coriander can be added alongside the parsley for a different herbal character. A small amount of dried lime (loomi) can be added with the stock for extra depth.
Khoresh karafs keeps for 2 days in the fridge and freezes well. Add the lemon juice after reheating rather than before storing, as it loses brightness with time.

Khoresh karafs is a standard entry in the Persian khoresh repertoire alongside fesenjan and ghormeh sabzi. It is seen as a lighter, spring-friendly stew and is a familiar fixture at family tables in Iran. The herbal generosity in the dish is characteristic of Persian cooking, where greens are used in volume rather than as garnish.
